title: Relevance Ranking
summary: Scoring and ordering matches so the best result lands first — TF-IDF, BM25, and the boosting signals layered on top of raw text relevance.

slides.markdown:
Finding documents that match a query is only half the job — an [inverted index](inverted-index) can tell you *which* documents contain the words, but not which one the user actually wants first. **Ranking** is the algorithm that scores every match and orders them, and it's the part users actually judge a search engine on.

Think of two restaurant reviews both mentioning "great pasta" — one is a two-line comment, the other a five-paragraph rave that says "pasta" six times. A good ranking function knows the second is the stronger match, without anyone hand-labeling it.

slides.sectionTitle: Why matching isn't enough — ranking is the real product
slides.markdown:
A boolean match ("does this document contain the query terms?") treats every matching document as equally good, which almost never reflects reality. A query for "apple" might match a fruit blog, a tech news article, and a legal filing that mentions the company once in a footnote — all technically matches, wildly different in relevance.

Users rarely look past the first handful of results, so the ordering *is* the product: two search engines with the identical inverted index can feel completely different in quality purely based on ranking. This is why ranking gets its own dedicated machinery rather than being an afterthought bolted onto matching.

slides.sectionTitle: TF-IDF: term frequency weighted by rarity
slides.markdown:
**TF-IDF** scores a term's importance to a document using two signals multiplied together. **Term frequency (TF)** — how often the term appears in this document; more mentions of "pasta" suggests a document is more about pasta. **Inverse document frequency (IDF)** — how rare the term is across the whole collection; a term like "the" appears everywhere and carries almost no signal, while a rare term like "sourdough" appearing at all is a strong signal.

Multiplying them means a term scores highly only if it's both frequent in this document *and* rare across the collection — exactly the terms that distinguish this document from the rest. TF-IDF was the dominant scoring approach for decades and is still a useful mental model even where it's been replaced by BM25.

**BM25** keeps TF-IDF's core idea — frequent-but-rare terms score higher — but fixes two practical problems. First, raw term frequency has diminishing returns: a document saying "pasta" 20 times isn't 20x more about pasta than one saying it once, so BM25 saturates TF with a curve instead of scaling linearly. Second, it normalizes for **document length**: a long document naturally contains more term mentions just by being long, so BM25 penalizes raw frequency in longer documents relative to the collection's average length.

BM25 is the default scoring function in Elasticsearch and Lucene today specifically because these two fixes make it behave better on real, uneven document collections than plain TF-IDF.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: two documents scored and ranked for the same query
slides.markdown:
![Two documents scored for the same query, ranked by score](assets/relevance-scoring.svg)

Both documents match the query, but they don't score equally: term frequency, rarity, and length normalization combine into a single numeric score per document, and results are simply sorted by that score, highest first.

The score itself is meaningless in isolation — it only matters relative to other documents' scores for the *same* query, which is why you'll never see a raw BM25 score shown to an end user.

slides.sectionTitle: Boosting signals: recency, popularity, field weighting
slides.markdown:
Pure text relevance (BM25) is rarely the whole ranking function in production — it's combined with **boosting signals** that reflect things text scoring can't see. **Recency** — a news search should favor today's article over one from 2019 that happens to score slightly higher on term match. **Popularity** — a product with 10,000 reviews and a 4.5-star rating is often a better answer than an obscure listing with a marginally better text match. **Field weighting** — a term match in a document's title usually matters more than the same term buried in a body paragraph, so titles get a higher weight multiplier.

These signals are typically blended as a weighted combination on top of the base BM25 score, tuned per product based on what users actually click.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: pure text relevance vs learning-to-rank with ML signals
slides.markdown:
As products mature, ranking often moves from hand-tuned formulas to learned models.

| | Pure text relevance (BM25 + boosts) | Learning-to-rank (ML) |
|---|---|---|
| How it scores | Fixed formula plus manually weighted signals | Model trained on labeled or click data |
| Signals used | Term frequency, rarity, recency, popularity | All of those, plus dozens more (CTR, dwell time, personalization) |
| Tuning | Manual weight adjustment | Retrained as behavior data accumulates |
| Data needed | None beyond the documents themselves | Large volume of query/click/relevance data |
| Best for | New products, cold start, no usage data yet | Mature products with enough traffic to train on |

**How to decide:** start with BM25 plus a few hand-tuned boosts — it needs no training data and is easy to reason about. Move to learning-to-rank once you have enough click data that a model can out-perform hand-tuned weights, not before.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: ranking by recency alone and burying the actually relevant result
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Newer is always more relevant, so let's just sort search results by publish date."

**Why it's wrong:** recency is one useful signal, not a replacement for text relevance. Sorting purely by date means a brand-new document that barely mentions the query terms outranks a highly relevant, comprehensive document from last month — users searching for an authoritative answer get a thin, unrelated result at the top.

**Correct model:** treat recency as one weighted input into a combined score, not the sort key itself — blend it with text relevance (BM25) so a document has to be both reasonably relevant *and* reasonably fresh to rank highly, with the exact weight tuned to the product (recency matters far more for news than for reference documentation).
